prize_parts.citation: For the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are lipid self-assembly and phase behaviour turned into a technology. A lipid whose headgroup pKa is tuned to be near neutral in blood and charged in the acidic endosome allows efficient nucleic-acid encapsulation, stable particles in circulation, and membrane destabilisation and release inside the cell. That is a clear physical-chemical principle (charge-dependent packing, non-lamellar phase propensity, fusion) with a verified molecular design rule, and it made siRNA drugs and mRNA vaccines deliverable at global scale. The Vancouver work by Cullis, Madden and Hope on loading, ionizable lipids and formulation is foundational, the evidence is independent and clinical, and the timing is right. The 2023 Medicine prize honoured nucleoside modification, not the delivery chemistry, so the two are separable. After comparing the openings I move this to first place and my own opening first choice, B059, to the first alternative, because colleagues' maturity arguments about B059 are fair and B064 has a firmer settled core.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the weak point. MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer made real contributions (SNALP clinical translation, lipid libraries, ionizable-lipid optimisation), and much of the optimised lipid chemistry used in approved products was developed in industry and is entangled with patents. A three-person cut limited to Vancouver may look like an academic-priority judgement the committee cannot fully verify. There is also an argument that this is formulation engineering with a thin discovery core, and that the headline impact depends on an mRNA application already prized in Medicine in 2023. I take that seriously and cannot dismiss it.

responses.point: Daniel Aili ranks B064 first as chemistry-driven enabling technology (pKa-tuned ionizable lipids, PEG-lipids, microfluidic mixing) that the 2023 Medicine prize did not cover, with Cullis, Hope and Madden as the core.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the separation from the 2023 prize, and he has moved me from B059 to B064 as first choice. I would press him on the claim that the credit is clean: much of the key ionizable-lipid optimisation (DLin-MC3-DMA and later lipids) is closely tied to MacLachlan and to Anderson and Langer's library work, so the citation should be worded around the design principle and early formulation rather than any single product. I want to know whether he would accept Cullis alone, or Cullis plus Madden, if the committee cannot defend a three-name split.

responses.point: Peter Brzezinski ranks B032 first but is cautious about B059, saying the concept is widely adopted yet still debated on mechanism, on what counts as phase separation in vivo, and may be early for a prize.
responses.response: This is the critique that most changed my view, because I made the same caveat in my own opening. As a physical chemist I find the demixing thermodynamics solid, but the claim that condensates are functional compartments in living cells rests partly on overexpression and in vitro reconstitution, and the Pappu and Mittag omission is a real attribution problem. Where I differ with him is B032: Gray and Winkler's work is rigorous and mature, but it extends a Marcus-type picture already recognised in 1992 and would be a late recognition of an established area, so I rank it below B064 and B059.

responses.point: Heiner Linke ranks nanopore sensing (B050) first as a clean single-molecule physical principle that became portable sequencing, with B059 second, and notes that B059 maturity is moderate but the concept is generative.
responses.response: I share his view that B059 is a generative, quantitative concept, and I keep it as my first alternative. On B050 I agree the science is excellent, but I am not persuaded it should outrank B064, since the attribution is difficult (Branton and Kasianowicz fall outside the three-name cut, and Deamer and Branton's priority needs checking) and the chemistry content is largely instrumentation and engineered pores. I would ask him which three names he can defend if the committee insists on tracing the original proposal to its source.

responses.point: Johan Aqvist ranks base editing (B058) first and Car-Parrinello (B014) second, citing the clean two-person credit for B014 and four decades of validation.
responses.response: I agree that B014 has the cleanest attribution on the list and I keep it as an alternative, and I accept the point that computational chemistry has been honoured before only if the committee considers the method rather than the field. Where I disagree is placing B058 first: with CRISPR recognised in 2020 and Kondo and Nishida's deaminase work a real priority competitor, I think a Liu-only prize is possible but more exposed than B064. I would like him to say how he would handle the Kondo and Nishida claim in a citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend a Cullis, Madden and Hope split against MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, or should prefer a narrower citation
How much of the ionizable-lipid design principle is academic discovery versus industrial optimisation
Whether the overlap with the 2023 Medicine mRNA prize is judged acceptable
Whether B059 will mature enough in the committee's view to outrank B064
statement.conflict_note: My research on lipid self-assembly and membranes is in the same broad field as B064 and B059, and I am a Lund colleague of Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, but no personal, institutional or collaborative connection to any candidate is apparent from the provided profile, so no specific conflict is apparent.
